title: Workflows vs. agents: who owns the next step

items.stem: In a fixed workflow, code decides the step order in advance; in an agent, who decides what happens next as it runs?

options.text: The program's code, chosen before the request arrives
The model, picking its own action each time
Whichever tool was listed first in the code
The user, confirming each step before it happens

items.stem: A support bot runs the same three steps in order every time: look up the account, check the plan, then have a model draft the reply. Workflow or agent?

options.text: Agent — a language model writes one of the steps
Agent — it calls tools to fetch data
Workflow — because the model never makes real choices
Workflow — the order of steps is fixed by code

items.stem: Checking whether the laser cutter is free tomorrow always takes one step: call check_calendar. Why does a fixed workflow suit the decision this task needs better than an agent?

options.text: Workflows are always cheaper to run than agents
An agent would end up calling check_calendar anyway
The steps never change, so there is nothing to decide
A fixed workflow can still branch based on what it finds

items.stem: A 3D print fails, and which checks to run next depends on what each earlier check finds. Why does an agent suit the decision needed better than a workflow?

options.text: The order can't be written into code ahead of time
Agents need less code to set up than workflows
A fixed workflow can only ever call one tool
Agents always produce more accurate answers than workflows

items.stem: Checking whether a student is trained on the laser cutter always takes one step: look up their training record. Why does this fit a fixed workflow better than an agent?
A student's question isn't in the manual; the assistant must judge which section to check next from what it finds. Why is an agent the better fit than a workflow?
